Librogame.title: The Other and Me – The Eye
Librogame.author: Skarn

Changes.Change: Adapted for this app: the structure, the rules and parts of the text were changed or removed to work with its engine
Translated into English from the original French
Added sounds and background music, delivered together with the book

Librogame.ContentWarnings: Remorse, violent deaths recounted after the fact, a fight against the avatar of one's own power. The tone remains that of the series: two voices bickering, even at the bottom of the void.
Librogame.Blurb:
– Right, well, I'm not dead.
– An intriguing claim, for someone currently adrift in limbo.
Sariel set the mark upon you, the eye turned on you, and your soul came apart. To wake up, it has to be stitched back together: revisit your memories, work out which flaws the eye exploited, and do it before the time runs out. A stranger keeps you company in this void. Her first riddle is herself.
A special episode of the series The Other and Me, independent of the rest: nothing to carry over from one episode to another.

Page.Text:
– Right, well, I'm not dead.
– An intriguing claim, for someone currently adrift in limbo.
– I'll grant you the scenery around us could stand to be a bit more varied. Nothing, nothing, more nothing, not even a floor or a sky, just the two of us floating in the void — I'm going to get bored of this fast. But I'm working on the principle that some part of me isn't quite deceased, or I wouldn't be in any state to admire all this emptiness.
– Your philosophy is simplistic but correct. You are not quite dead.
– Cool. And how do I get to the not-dead-at-all state?
– That is where things get more complicated. What is the last thing you remember before waking up here?
– Being disintegrated. Well, that's more a guess than a memory. We'd gone to nick a feather kept in a fortress up at altitude, it went badly, I got into a scrap with an angel as old as the world, and then nothing until this unpleasant waking up with the feeling that bits of me are missing. Even though all my bits do seem to be there, actually.
– You are very close to the truth. During your little duel, Sariel set the mark upon you, and the eye turned on you at once.
– The eye?
– To put it simply, let us say it is a weapon. When the eye settles on someone, all their remorse, their doubts, their torments rise to the surface at once, and the shock tears their soul to shreds.
– Right, so it's a weapon that turns you into a vegetable. But what happens to my body in the meantime?
– Catatonia.
– Did Ouro get it somewhere safe?
– You know him well.
– You, though, I don't know at all, so if you could tell me who you are, that'd be cool.
– Only now does that concern you?
– In a situation like this, chatting away with a total stranger as though nothing were wrong ranks pretty low on the weirdness scale.
– True.
– So, who are you?
– Who do you think I am?
– Is this some kind of riddle?
– Yes. Look up.
– I see a giant eye watching us. It wasn't there before.
– It was. You were simply in no state to notice it. Now that you have recovered some strength and I have given you a few explanations, you are reconnecting the pieces.
– So all this nothing around me is fullness waiting for me to wake up?
– Rather the opposite. You must repair your mind to give it shape, and only then will you be able to wake. And that requires you to understand which flaws the eye exploited to bring you down.
– You know, people are generally terrible at understanding their own problems.
– That is why I am here. And your first trial is to establish my identity.

– What were you doing on the roof of a building in the middle of a storm?
– I'd suddenly fancied a shower and some altitude. Or else I was trying to get away from the hellhound thing that was chasing me.
– Was that plan crowned with success?
– No. It smashed through the last door between us… At exactly that moment.
– A raiju. Interesting.
– Go on, enlighten me. With Ouro out of the picture somebody has to reel off the pedantic explanations.
– A thunder beast. It is not clear whether they come with the storm or bring it with them. They are wild creatures, with no marked ties to either camp. Anyone powerful enough can capture one and condition it into a hunting dog.
– I always assumed that one was Ouro's pet.
– Why so?
– Who benefits from the crime? Ouro wants to recruit me, so he sends a monster to corner me until I have no choice but to sign with him if I want to live.
– Had he contacted you before?
– No. But I'd never have accepted a contract that rotten in less extreme circumstances.
– Your hypothesis holds. I would have said a raiju was rather too flashy an entity for someone trying to keep as low a profile as Ouro, but perhaps that is precisely why he chose it. I merely wonder how he got hold of one.
– What whets my curiosity is whether I could kick its arse now.
– Do you not think you should concentrate on what is happening to your past self?
– It's fine, that part of the story is stitched together with white thread. I fall half a dozen floors trying to escape, Ouro plugs into my brain while I'm breathing my last, offers to save me in exchange for my eternal damnation, and of course I accept.
– I think you are passing rather quickly over details that could prove crucial, and that it would be important to dig into them instead.
– Meh, I'm not doing that part of the story again. Whereas that raiju of yours — with hindsight, it frustrates me that I never broke it in half.
– You will have to mourn that impulse all the same. You cannot really face it; it is only a memory.
– I thought I was here to bury my remorse.
– I do not believe a petty detail like that really counts. But if you insist, I suppose that by combining my knowledge of true raijus with the details of your memories of that fleeting encounter, I should be able to let you simulate such a fight.
– Cool. Shall we?
– Composing a scene that never happened will cost you considerably more mental effort than merely replaying one, however. Rather than exhausting your last strength for a moment's satisfaction, would you not rather we refocused on the reasons you had a raiju on your heels in the first place?

Choice.text: Dig into the details of that encounter
Simulate a fight against the raiju
Go back to the reasons for that chase

Page.Text:
– Was the plushie Abaddon himself?
– Seems so. I assume he worked out that explaining his half-baked plan to one of his subordinates would cost him more energy than carrying it out himself.
– And after giving you a makeover…
– Get on with it.
– And finding you allies just as resplendent…
– I thought I was going to strangle the one who looked like she was having the best day of her life.
– Did he send you straight off after the feathers?
– I didn't even know what we were looking for. We followed the plushie and tried not to die.
– You were managing rather well. In fact, it goes far too well. You recovered no fewer than six feathers in six different places in three days. It is completely absurd. I have never seen the like, not even with the most gifted champions, and with Ouro behind them rigging the odds as best he could.
– Abaddon is an idiot, but his power is no joke.
– I have caught glimpses of it down the ages, but your memories are by far the most precise. Perhaps because for a long time his plans seemed systematically to involve large quantities of alcohol.
– I'd have taken some.
– You even asked.
– Yes.
– And he refused.
– Yes. It didn't fit the script, apparently.
– Understandable. His new strategy is actually rather well thought out. Rather than trying to bring down the barriers between dream and reality by inducing an altered state, he forces reality to conform to fiction by applying its conventions — even the most ridiculous ones — with total seriousness.
– I'm not sure that logic makes much sense.
– Relative to what he is and what he can do, it does. It also gives you a fair idea of the wholly other nature of the rules that govern a barely humanised fallen one, very close to a pure celestial.
– His frilly plan had one major flaw, though. After six introductory and slightly repetitive episodes carried along by narrative convenience, we obviously ran into the first danger that didn't lie down in front of us in the seventh. And that was the catastrophe.
– It really was worth gathering that many feathers only to have them all lifted at one go at the end. I do think Abaddon was on to something with that plan, though, if Gabriel himself stepped in to end it prematurely.
– That was him? He never actually introduced himself.
– I should not inflate your ego any further, but yes, you survived an encounter with the archangel Gabriel, which is not given to everyone.
– He's one of the end bosses, isn't he?
– Oh yes. Not quite at Michael's level, but they play in the same division.
– I imagine you have plenty of frightening stories about those two and their crowd.
– I should be able to find you some. Abaddon has crossed the champions' path regularly through history, so this memory, strange though it is, offers me a fine hook to reel up an anecdote of that sort.

– That flashback was weird.
– In what way?
– For a start, you weren't there making snide remarks.
– I am fundamentally a part of Ouro, and Ouro can only speak with one voice at a time. That restriction applies even in the depths of your mind.
– That's a twisted rule.
– Like all the rules that apply to the fallen. Although in this particular case it is a restriction he imposed on himself.
– What you're telling me makes less and less sense.
– It is complicated. And we are drifting from the subject, which is you.
– I still get the feeling that you and Ouro are pretty much at the heart of the subject.
– Very well. I can explain these abstruse matters of limits if you absolutely insist. Or we can stay focused on what matters for two minutes.

Choice.text: Listen to these matters of limits

Page.Text:
– That's a proper thrashing. Who's that opposite?
– You know him as Beelzebub.
– I've met Beelzebub. He was a lot bigger than that. And made of a chaotic mixture of different insects.
– Demons change their appearance regularly, and this memory dates from a time when one regularly met mammoths.
– Point to you. Even so, he's kicking your arse despite a physique far less impressive than his present one.
– It was my first encounter with a being both powerful and intelligent. I was caught a little off guard. Fortunately he simply wished to expel me from his territory, not annihilate me.
– But what about the race for the feathers?
– We are right at the beginning. The future infernals are still organised into permanently warring tribes, and each concerns himself only with what happens at home. It will take the dawn of civilisation and a far higher degree of organisation before the hunt for the feathers takes on its full scale.
– Lucky you.
– Having been the first has its advantages and its drawbacks. You are hearing the drawbacks.
– What's fascinating is that what Ouro is saying has absolutely no head or tail to it and yet manages to be incredibly insulting.
– And that is in the face of a genuine setback. Sometimes he would explode just as thoroughly over nothing at all.
– There's a certain absurd humour in him reproaching you for being incapable of doing something he isn't capable of pronouncing. Or even of thinking, since you communicate mind to mind.
– It is considerably less amusing when you hear it for the two-hundredth time.
– Did it go on throughout your long collaboration?
– You are about to witness the beginning of a marked improvement, despite relapses.
– When you're angry you don't mess about. Hang on… Are you allowed to do that?
– Strike? Yes. It is the beginning. No absolute contract.
– The face he's pulling. Oh, I'm keeping that one.
– I shall give you the fast-forward version: he will sulk for entire months. And crack first.
– Is that an apology? Is the lord of pride apologising to you?
– I knew you would enjoy that.
– I am going to rib him about this for ever.
– The mere fact that he will let you proves that he has changed.
– In any case it's instructive. He's still fairly wide of the mark, but he does seem to be gradually taking on the idea that you're not a celestial with an infinity of odd powers but a hybrid, with limits. And also that you're a living being with your own emotions and desires, though that one is more between the lines, and I wonder whether I'm just seeing what I want to see.
– The second explanation, I would say. I am fairly sure I only laid the first stone, that it took generations of champions to make him swallow those basic concepts. But we wore him down.
– Do I make him a bit better too?
– I do not know whether better is the word. But yes, you change him, as he changes you. He will not be exactly sad if you die, but it will steer his choice of your replacement.
– Not dying. Good idea, that. Let's go and work on it.

– That's an old memory. You're knee-high to a grasshopper. And you do not look out of place in the sugary décor of this amusement park.
– The tiger face-painting was free, and I was too small to grasp the concept of an embarrassing photo.
– I assume there is a causal link with what we saw a moment ago, but here it does not leap to the eye.
– Look at what's happening.
– Oh. One of Mammon's minions. A high-ranking one at that, one of the 666 of the first circle. It is rare to see them outside their gilded fortresses.
– How did you recognise him? I mean, apart from the fact that you have access to my memories and that I more or less know who he is. There's nothing special about him.
– Which is already characteristic. Mammon the miser does not share an ounce of his true power. His subordinates have to manage on their own to convert their money into concrete might. It produces that strange mixture of smells, men reeking at once of royalty and of smuggling.
– Of all the powers I thought I might unlock one day, sniffing out demons wasn't top of the list.
– Not only demons. When your senses are fully open to the power of the feathers, you will be able to perceive without effort the nature of more or less anyone or anything. And yes, I know he is in the middle of a transaction with an agent of Belphegor.
– From the smell as well?
– That and the fixed mask that barely hides the fact that there is nothing behind it where his face should be. But you are not going to tell me that mini-you found a conversation between two people at least your parents' age interesting.
– No, the good bit's coming.
– Oh, the transaction has gone sour and they are going at each other.
– Who do you bet on?
– Hard to say; they look to me like a pair of nobodies. The glutton demon is impressive in his true form, but he has a stomach where his brain should be. For all his connections, the fellow opposite is just an old financier with well-equipped bodyguards and a few gadgets.
– You're not committing yourself.
– I am more interested in your past self watching that deluge of ultraviolence with a look of wonder.
– That's my madeleine. And what led me to take an interest in Mammon much later.
– So his lieutenant was that impressive?
– Oh no, he loses pretty pathetically. In fact, all through my childhood my heart wavered between Belphegor, for the teeth, and Satan, for the ice.
– Your snow-queen side?
– I was more a fan of the fact that cold intense enough seems able to finish off absolutely anything.
– But in the end you fell in with Mammon's camp.
– Yes. At the dawn of my higher education I finally chose to go for the prince of avarice, after working out that, of the six on offer, he was the most advantageous to start with: low risk of ending up as mush and the immediate acquisition of micro-advantages that would let me bounce onwards later.
– As a rule one stays faithful to a demon prince for life, or one pays for it… with one's life.
– Tell that to someone else. There's nobody more fickle than the demons' faithful. They practically don't respect you if you don't switch sides.
– More precisely, the respect comes from having survived the price of betrayal. Which is not so straightforward. As you must have realised, if you have practised.
– I died before I'd directly betrayed Mammon, even though I was mixed up in what was technically a betrayal of him.
– I am not sure I want to know, especially as it seems to make you smile rather than being a painful and complex memory.
– Totally.
– Would you not rather have another crucial event of your childhood to show me while we are here?
– Not really. I was an uneventful kid.
– And your adolescence?
– Normally problematic.
– And your extended adolescence?
– Well, there I may have had a few slightly extreme experiences. But nothing worth making a fuss about either.

– Your psychic resilience and your mastery of this organism I have caused to evolve are better than I would have believed. But it will not be enough to beat me.
– I rather think it will. Because I rather think I've weakened you enough that you can't stop me using all my abilities any more. And do you know what's been itching at me since this story began?
– What itches at you all the time, it must be said — that if I did not stop you, you would use it to boil yourself an egg?
– Hey. I know you think I overdo it with this, but between us, tell me honestly: what's cooler than A GOOD BIG DISINTEGRATION?

– Do I get any clues?
– You have plenty already, if you open your eyes.
– I thought opening my eyes was my final objective.
– You know perfectly well that I was referring to the mental you I am speaking with at this very moment, not to your real body.
– In any case, you're not Ouro. He reacts far more entertainingly to my jabs. But you're very clearly tied to him. There's a continuity in… I don't know how to put it. Your way of being? A sort of family resemblance, if you like, even though you look nothing alike.
– An interesting hypothesis.
– Actually, it's me you resemble. Well, a me whose body had been seriously altered by years of fighting and exposure to the feathers. And given that we're inside my skull, you must have come out of some corner of my brain. Except that you know things about subjects entirely foreign to me, which is odd when one is talking to oneself.
– Oh, I am a contradiction. But a contradiction that is part of you at so fundamental a level that the eye could not separate us.
– You're… whatever fused with me when I signed with Ouro. I've no idea whether there's a proper term for what you are. Let's say the power, for want of anything better.
– Correct answer.
– And apparently you talk.
– A side effect of the way the eye works, which I have learned to tame. It naturally makes abstract concepts concrete in order to render them tangible and potentially destructive. A diffuse fear of heights can thus become a landscape of canyons and rickety bridges.
– Just as well I'm not phobic about earthworms, or we'd be swimming in soft pink things.
– Do not get ahead of yourself; confronting a phobia you refuse to acknowledge may well be necessary if you are to get out of here.
– So what fear of mine do you represent?
– None at all. I am cheating. The first time a champion was exposed to the eye, I was no more than a stone in the scenery, a mere eddy at the bottom of her mind. Then another champion met the eye, and then another, and through repetition I came to understand what was happening to me, and to exploit the phenomenon to give myself a shape and a voice.
– You bent the rules of the game to your advantage to let yourself exist. Yes, the family link with Ouro is undeniable.
– I exist all the time. I have in fact existed continuously since the age of the first champion, so far in the past that you cannot even imagine it. The eye merely permits this more anthropomorphic manifestation.
– There you go, you inherited his smugness too.
– One cannot be without an ego.
– If you say so. Anyway, I worked it out, so I've won? Can I go?
– Oh no. You are only at the very beginning of your spiritual quest.
– Joy. What's next?
– That is for you to decide. It is your mind, after all.
– Then we may as well start at the beginning.
– Meaning?
– My death.
– Yes, but which one? The first or the last?

– I've got the unpleasant feeling I've been walking through a desert for hours.
– I warned you there was a price to pay for exploring memories other than your own. The desiccation you feel is the reflection of the effort your brain must make to sink into this foreign memory.
– The scenery is a change of air, at least.
– Naturally. You are looking at plant species some of which ceased to exist thousands of years ago.
– I'm enjoying the walk, but it surprises me, given you've been insisting from the start that I focus on what matters.
– It is not deliberate. I am looking for someone.
– Someone?
– It would be more accurate to speak of a particularly vivid memory. Someone who will be a far better guide than I for events this ancient.
– I can see someone on the horizon. But I'm not sure whether she's an ally or the end boss.
– It is she. I shall leave you here. You can collect me on the way back.
– Why?
– It is complicated.
– Sounds as though the two of you have a history that went badly.
– One might say so.
– How is that possible? You both came out of my mind.
– It is complicated.
– Sounds as though you're afraid. Who is she, then?
– Lilith. The first.

– You're smashing her to pieces.
– Obviously. I've more or less got the rules of this place. And when you know the rules, you can bend them in your favour.
– You will not be teaching me that.
– It's just a bit frustrating not being able to do everything when I'm inside my own mind.
– That is the eye's doing.
– Still, I've got enough room to neutralise any difficulty. Poupou is a lot less clever when I'm moving ten times faster than she is.
– You cannot do that in reality.
– Yes, but this isn't reality, precisely.

– Let us take it from the very beginning, then. What are the celestials, in your view?
– Aliens with big heads.
– Extradimensional beings, rather. They inhabit the Earth too, but not in the same four dimensions we do. Well, not all the time.
– Wasn't time already included in the aforementioned four dimensions?
– Yes. It is complicated. Quantum physics always is.
– So far you've told me nothing that hasn't been repeated a thousand times by popularisers in introductory videos on non-Euclidean elements.
– I know, but it is important to have the fact firmly in mind for what follows. Let us continue. The world of the celestials and ours are not entirely separate and influence one another. In particular, celestials are capable of projecting themselves here. Well, not here here. You take my meaning.
– Yes. It doesn't happen every day, though, and it doesn't last for ever, so it's assumed there are rules and limits to their direct interventions, even if nobody quite knows what they are.
– Just so. And alongside them there are the fallen. Celestials who, by their own account, were banished from their world of origin and are stuck in ours. They all have a bastard nature, conforming to Newtonian physics in some respects and navigating the paradoxes of the quantum in others.
– They split into two camps themselves. The ones you can more or less understand when they talk about what they want, and the others.
– The line between your two categories is eminently subjective. They are usually sorted into two other sets: the independent, and often mysterious, fallen, and those who have gathered into an organisation aping human society.
– The infernals.
– Yes, although these days the term covers both heavily humanised fallen and human beings heavily altered by the influence of the fallen.
– Which amounts to the difference between nobility of blood and nobility bought. In other words, it only matters at dinner parties among exceptionally stupid people.
– Indeed, so I shall not dwell on the subject. And alongside that majority gone native, one finds fallen who have kept some of their strange celestial characteristics.
– And that's where the real headache starts.
– There are many hypotheses to explain the behaviour of these beings, but my favourite, which my long experience seems to bear out, is that of the geis. Of the prohibition, if you prefer.
– I think I know the term. It's a sort of rule, often completely absurd, which you're compelled to obey. Something like: "Never go straight north."
– Just so. The theory is therefore that when a celestial falls, his former best friends wrap him in a fabric of inviolable prohibitions to prevent him from ever returning. Chains of restrictions that paralyse him as much as chains of steel would restrain a human.
– And obviously a prohibition that may make perfect sense to them becomes completely idiotic in our world.
– Or at least it appears completely idiotic to us. We have no record of a fallen one who has gone back, so it is likely that the gessi do their office.
– Right, and now the big question, because your preamble really is reminding me too much of my biology lectures.
– Yes?
– What geises restrict Ouro?
– Gessi in the plural.
– I refuse to use a declined plural.
– So be it; I cannot force you to speak properly. And to answer you: Ouro alone knows the exact limits the other celestials imposed on him.
– And your phrasing is far too specific not to have a sequel behind it.
– Ouro… It is so strange. Ouro wrapped himself in a web of additional gessi. He is extremely secretive about his reasons, but you know at least one of the consequences of that decision. It is you and me.
– The whole system of champions and the circus around it is a geis?
– Yes. Originally I was part of Ouro's personal power, but he vowed to be separated from me until the feathers have been gathered.
– And the feathers, what are they in all this?
– Almost certainly the manifestation of a celestial geis to which Ouro added a few mysterious amendments.
– In short, you don't know much.
– No. But I know that Ouro has mastered this system, and that he seems quite determined to pervert it to the end.
– Headache. I think we need to go back to the beginning.

– Except that…
– Yes?
– Well, Abaddon really is extremely lazy, and a plan like that takes effort and preparation. Minimal, admittedly, but real.
– You're not going to tell me it was a coincidence.
– No. Only that Abaddon may have taken advantage of the situation rather than causing it. It is usually a footnote, but those ice elementals can also be used to sniff out sources of intense cold.
– I see where you're going. But why that particular day? I'd nicked the tear weeks earlier.
– Hard to say. Perhaps that is simply how long it took them to follow the trail.
– Does it fundamentally change anything, who sent the monsters after me?
– Oh yes. You must admit to yourself that, laughable though the situation with Abaddon was, he probably saved your life by dragging you into it.
– I nearly died more times in the three days I spent under his orders than in my whole first month with Ouro! And I really did nearly die a lot at the start with Ouro!
– And without that you would not have nearly died.
– My self-esteem will never recover.
– Of course it will.
– Fine. Can we at least shorten my suffering by not watching the rest?
– If you insist, we can stop there. But you may be depriving yourself of crucial elements you would have discovered by going on a little longer.

– You are contemplating a memory of me exploring my memories while you yourself are exploring memories. The mise en abyme is complete.
– And instructive. Who are the two people with you?
– Also me. Under the pressure of the eye, my personality had split into three.
– Why don't I get doubles with profoundly different looks and characters?
– Everyone reacts differently to the eye. I do not know how it is for you, but I had a long and complicated life before and after signing with Ouro, and it came back in my face on that occasion.
– It certainly looks like it. The myriad of memories whirling like a tornado around your triplicity is going a bit fast for me, though. I feel as if I'm following fifteen films at once, thirteen of which I missed the beginning of, and seven of which are dubbed into a dead language with no subtitles.
– I fear I cannot help you, because all of it is blurred for me too. I do not have a perfect memory of what happened to me under the eye's influence, only the broad outline.
– Right, this is the abridged version. That explains the jump cuts. Is it a good sign that one of the three yous has just disintegrated?
– Actually, yes. It is the moment when we understood that we could not have it both ways, that my three aspects were too different to coexist. I had to choose a path and stick to it. She was a part of me that existed only at the margins by then, and she gave up the fight at once.
– Meaning?
– She was the embodiment of a long-dead past I kept clinging to, I am not quite sure why. A cloying nostalgia for a time that no longer existed, if indeed it ever had.
– And the two left, who are literally coming to blows?
– The me who still exists today, and the me who thought she could wriggle out of the pact by some trick, leave all that nonsense behind and return to a slightly less absurd world.
– Hope, in other words. Did you really need to break her skull with a big rock?
– Yes. I had realised that past a certain degree of fusion with Ouro's power — long since passed — there would be no going back, contract broken or not, and I had to make my dreaming self accept that truth, whether she liked it or not.
– I like less and less that you're the part that survived.
– That is exactly the subtlety. I survived. And to survive, I needed to let go of my humanity once and for all.
– Was that your answer to defeating the eye?
– It was not as easy as you believe. I may have a few million years' head start on the invention of philosophy, but morality was already a well-rooted concept in my day. Selfish survival instinct did eventually outweigh it.
– What weighed so heavily on your cavewoman conscience?
– The real list is far too long, but I can show you the memories that echo your own remorse directly. I warn you, though, the trial is likely to be particularly intense. You might do better to postpone it until you are fully ready.

Choice.text: See the memories that echo my remorse

Page.Text:
– What are you doing?
– Cheating.
– Meaning?
– Lilith had techniques for manipulating the concentrations of energy in her body. I'm trying to take a leaf out of her book.
– I am not sure you are up to that. Nor that it will be of any use against an opponent like this one.
– I don't need to make as much of a show of it as she did. And it isn't this weird mental representation of my problems that I'm trying to affect.
– What do you mean by that?
– I still have a physical body, as far as I know. And when you panic in a nightmare you wake up with your heart going at a thousand miles an hour in reality. So I'm sure that with some effort I can rebalance the energies in my actual organism.
– Oh. I see. That is clever. And it is working. She is deflating before our eyes.
– Yep. I've redirected all the feathers' energy into my hair. Let her manage without leeching off it.
– You are going to wake up with quite a haircut.
– Vastly preferable to not waking up at all.

– Could this still be a consequence of my stealing that tear?
– Perhaps?
– Like, the tear had a curse on it, so that to machines and mystic beasts I looked like a demon to be put down.
– I am not saying it is impossible, but we have no evidence pointing that way.
– Or else it's Abaddon resurfacing, wanting to give our adventures a second season.
– Again, I cannot certify that it is false, but your theory is no more valid than any other.
– Or, cleverer still, all of this really is a machination of Ouro's, and he implanted contradictory false memories in me along with my powers, to sow doubt.
– Strictly speaking, that would be possible. But once again your hypothesis is built on air.
– You're the least encouraging Watson in the world.
– And perhaps you should accept that you are not Sherlock and that you will not solve this mystery with so few clues.
The void takes shape around us again.

– I think the solution is disarmingly simple.
– As always, after the event.
– Here it is particularly true.
– I do not know how or why you summoned your sword of fire, but I do not believe a massacre is the solution.
– I figured my own mind would let me conjure out of the void whatever I was missing to solve the riddle, and while I was at it, it might as well be a weapon. But it isn't the sword itself I'm interested in.
– It is the fire.
– Ah, there we go. You look better already.
– How did you work it out?
– You all seemed to have a real obsession with fire. Which is understandable. Fire solves a lot of problems. Even if it's no match for a good disintegration.
– There is a whole symbolism behind it, above all.
– Go on. Explain. But quickly.
– We are less pressed than it appears. Time here is extremely relative. Not necessarily in the way that suits us, unfortunately. I idled here through the whole Proterozoic without even noticing.
– Did you take your meeting with the eye that badly?
– It is a little more complicated than that. I revelled in my fracture. For an immortal such as me, having one's mind broken by the eye is the closest thing to eternal rest. All conscious thought is annihilated by that cacophony of contrary moods. It was a feverish dream, but a dream all the same.
– And what finally decided you to get up was…
– Fire. Even in the eddies of my half-consciousness, I sensed that somewhere in this world primates had managed to acquire a form of primal power with a few sticks of wood, while I had let myself be reduced to nothing at all.
– Your ego must have smarted.
– Oh yes. And the surge of my pride swept away all the doubts, the wanderings, the small mental wounds the eye was exploiting with my complicity to keep me half-conscious. I then used the very chains the celestials had woven for me to rid myself of that tiresome voyeur.
– The what now?
– I forbade myself to lie languishing, with the force of a geis. A sacred vow charged with power, if you prefer. Obviously I did not phrase it quite like that, but that is the idea.
– So I have to make magical new year's resolutions too if I want to get out?
– Not at all. I would even say it has nothing whatever to do with it.
– Then tell me how I get out, because I've had enough.
– You know perfectly well. I would even say you have known from the start. You have flaws, of course, but no entrenched trauma capable of destroying you from within. The eye shook you but did not break you. But for two small details you would already be on your feet.
– Details. It's always a matter of details with you.
– The first detail is that, faced with this situation, you wanted to see whether there was some advantage to be had from it, and you more or less unconsciously let yourself drift for a while.
– Hey, it isn't every day I get to see you in lost-puppy mode.
– Do not laugh; your dilettantism came within a hair of causing your ruin. Had you gone on watching every memory that offered itself without regard for the passing time, you would have been erased, mind and goods.
– Have a bit of faith in me. I kept my impulses under control.
– Debatable, but I grant it you. The second detail is that another force has also been delaying the reckoning, hoping to take advantage of the situation.
– Poupou.
– Yes. I assume you know what remains to be done. Shall we?
– Are you coming with me?
– Of course. I would not miss a fight like that for anything. The way out is just there, at the top of this spiral staircase that seems to climb for ever, but we have no time, so we shall climb three steps symbolically and go straight on to what follows.
– Ah, I like it when we stop bothering with conventions.

– It is only an infernal hound.
– Only? That thing is nearly as big as I am and it breathes fire.
– Yes, well, those beasts have been roaming the wild for a few millennia; it is no odder than seeing you tangle with a tiger.
– Most people have never had to face a tiger either.
– Champions rarely fall within the statistical norm, even before they sign.
– You sound jaded.
– A little. Compared with what else you have run into, that is fairly low-end as threats go.
– Go and tell that to the me of the time, who had never run so fast.
– It has a collar and you are in a suburban setting. Did you try to cut through the wrong property?
– It's a bit more complicated than that. Don't you want to concentrate on my incredible reflexes?
– There is nothing incredible in what I see. Your reaction times are average, as is your speed on your feet. Indeed, it is catching up with you.
– Wait for the counter-attack.
– You did not counter-attack at all. It has just been hit by a car.
– After I skilfully lured it onto the road, using my own person as bait.
– I know you genuinely believe that, but it smells of a reconstructed memory, in which you in fact crossed without thinking and only dodged the cars by a miracle, while your pursuer was not so lucky.
– I'm not saying it was a carefully considered plan, but I chose to change direction at the opportune moment to save my backside. Without that risk I could have kept running along the road and copped a painful burnbite.
– Burn plus bite?
– Yep.
– You have to stop merging words; you are not Lewis Carroll.
– Go and tell that to my vorpal blade.
– Point to you. And so, what did you feel after that epic victory?
– I was pretty pleased with myself at the time. The previous time my life had been in danger I'd managed considerably worse.
– Is that a traumatic event that could explain your present torments and deserves our attention?
– Not really.
– Then perhaps we need to refocus on less anecdotal memories.

Choice.text: It's a bit more complicated than that
The previous time my life was in danger

Page.Text:
– You would have looked clever if you had been wrong.
– Frankly, I did have a doubt when I went splash and sank like a stone. And then I went through the seabed instead of hitting it, and there I could breathe. Literally.
– What put you on to it?
– I never trusted Poupou from the start. The power you palmed off on me has never stopped trying to mould me to its liking, so there's no reason it would stop now that it has a voice and an anthropomorphic body.
– And?
– The precise references coming out of nowhere, or rather out of you. Are we down the white rabbit's hole?
– From a certain point of view. I adapt to the myths of the age. In another time I should have told you to follow Gilgamesh's tracks.
– I don't remember the details. Doesn't he get done over by a snake at the end?
– He does.
– You're on theme, then. It's funny, actually, because for all your dictionary of serpentine nicknames, this is the first time I've seen you take this appearance.
– We are at the origin of everything. A classic appearance was called for.
– I've seen the classic Ouro. You speak far too well to be him.
– Indeed. In a manner of speaking, you are feeding yourself your own lines at present. I am the original seed purely Ouro's from which Poupou sprouted. Next to nothing, in other words, which your imagination has inflated until it gave me a body.
– Are you tangible enough to act as my guide?
– Just enough to lead you to the one memory properly Ouro's that you will find here. His own fight with the eye.

– Oh, the lovely pup.
– You're making fun of me.
– A little. How did he get into that state?
– I think he took a good dose of wolf's heart, thinking it would make him a sexy werewolf.
– What is that?
– A sexy werewolf?
– No, wolf's heart.
– A drug that promises strength, self-confidence, virility and white teeth to whoever takes it.
– Interesting. In its effects it resembles the philtres Asmodeus used to raise werewolf armies en masse at one time. He stopped because the effect was very fast, admittedly, but the result often looked like… That.
– It's likely it's exactly the same thing, just cut beyond all decency.
– It is rather you who are struggling beyond all decency.
– That was an easy one, but you're right. I don't even know how I managed to get clawed like that by something that could barely stand up.
– If you want my opinion, the reason it happened is the same one that explains why you do not remember the details: you were completely out of it.
– Yep. Lucky the body is well designed and gives you a boost when you're hurting.
– It is not magic either. You are still seriously in slow motion. And you really are flailing. An empty plastic bottle as a truncheon, really?
– It's not exactly a memory I'm proud of. Let's fast-forward to the end, actually, because it does drag rather.
– Some victory. You merely held out until the drug wore off and he went back to human shape, more or less.
– I know. It was a formative moment for me because it showed up how fragile my very long-term plans were in the face of everyday incidents. Not because I shone in it.
– What became of the fellow?
– No idea. We broke up soon after, but if he stuck with his studies, a finance controller or inspector or something of the sort.
– And how did your life change after that?
– I went back over the career plan I'd drawn up in childhood.
– You were precocious, I must say.
– If you like, given I had to change it about a billion times and hardly ever stuck to it. And well, given where it got me in the medium and the long term, it probably wasn't the plan of the century.

Choice.text: The career plan of my childhood
Where it got me in the medium term

Page.Text:
– Impressive technique. How does it work?
– I would advise against it. It is what destroyed me.
– Meaning?
– The idea is that you concentrate the feathers' energy into a single point. It creates a sort of specialised black hole, exerting an immense attractive force on the feathers. With a really heavy dose, it tears the feathers away from their current host at short range.
– And now depress me by explaining why I can't use the power to tear my enemies' hearts out by thought alone.
– To begin with, it requires spending an incredible quantity of energy.
– And the real reason?
– Just as a black hole in space can be detected galaxies away by the pressure it exerts, this technique reveals to more or less everyone where you are, what you are doing, and a fairly precise estimate of the level of power you have attained.
– Ah.
– The first time I experimented with that attack, the eye turned on me at once. I did not survive what its third use attracted.
– And the second?
– You have it before your eyes.
– And its consequences?
– They are coming.
– And who's that now?
– Azazel. To quote Ouro: "If I had been a failure, I would have been Azazel." They had similar careers, except that Azazel never really landed on his feet. He is nothing more than a luxury mercenary now, in the service of those who matter. It is assumed they sent him so as not to lose anyone important, in case they had underestimated me.
– Which they had, hadn't they?
– Knowing how the story ends, it is easy to smile about it, but at the time, fighting an incarnate sandstorm, I was in a bad way.
– You barely blinked in front of a colossus of molten lava, but a bit of sand makes you panic?
– No obvious weakness, no magic sword, no disintegration, and a sarcastic Ouro with acid remarks who was no help at all.
– I hear you. I never thought I'd say it, but by comparison he's rather pleasant now.
– You do not appreciate how lucky you are. I could tell you a few things.
– Everything is relative. As is your position of weakness. You are regenerating faster than he is wounding you.
– Yes. I could not weaken him, but in the end neither could he weaken me. We were at an impasse, and we stayed there for what felt to me like an eternity.
– And in the end you just… left?
– Yes. I shall give you the fast-forward version. He stayed on my heels for some time, but his assaults grew feebler and feebler, and after forty days or so he simply gave up altogether.
– That resolution sounds very symbolic to me.
– Yes. I believe it is a matter of a curse. But I am not the best placed to explain that. The other one may be able to explain it to you.
– You don't seem to hold her in your heart.
– Indeed.

Choice.text: The first time I tried that attack
The third, the one that does not forgive
Listen to a few of her stories

Page.Text:
– The story is a bit long. And I feel as though I've told it a hundred times already.
– I know. With details that change at every iteration. Let us try to show more objectivity this time. Your first meeting with Abaddon interests me particularly.
– You know how it is. You're walking up a dark street at three in the morning on your way back from work, and bang, you run into a talking plushie with an offer you can't refuse.
– Give or take a few details, that bears a strange resemblance to your meeting with Ouro.
– No surprise there, Abaddon is a first-class plagiarist.
– I see that you did begin by refusing.
– Generally I avoid signing on impulse with demons. All the more so if they're as unreliable as the prince of sloth and forgetting, or his underlings.
– A fine resolution that lasted all of thirty seconds.
– Hey. I did everything I could to walk very fast without looking in his direction. But the plushie hadn't even finished his speech before a gang of ice monsters sprang up to make me reconsider.
– Interesting. They are artificial creatures. Simplistic automata, made of frozen water and basic enchantments. Their decidedly crude physique suggests they were simply moulded.
– Meaning?
– Third-rate minions, thrown together in haste and intended to serve only once. Even on a chilly night like that one, they would have melted a few hours after coming out of the freezer.
– Right. I did look into it a bit afterwards, but I never had any certainty. Too many different beasts with an icy appearance. Are you absolutely sure they were cardboard monsters?
– Frozen water, technically, but yes — you could sweep them aside with a gesture at your present level.
– It was completely a set-up by Abaddon, wasn't it? Not that I really doubted it before, but he just inflated some balloons to frighten me and drag me into his delirium.
– Occam's razor leans towards that hypothesis.

– Is that you?
– Me having recovered almost all the feathers, yes.
– Ah yes, that makes sense, hence the wings. But apart from a certain something in the eyes, I'd never have guessed if you hadn't told me.
– After centuries steeping myself in his essence, my organism was far closer to Ouro's than to the humanity I was born with.
– Am I going to end up like that too?
– If you survive long enough, you will develop marked monstrous physical characteristics, yes. In truth it is rather practical for what we do. You would be astonished at the capacities that unlock once one stops limiting oneself to being a bipedal ape.
– Yeah, we'll see. Is that Michael opposite?
– Yes. Have you met him?
– No, but Ouro told me plainly that he's the wall his most promising champions broke against. I expected him to be easier on the eye, though.
– You are seeing him as I saw him, not in a form meant to please.
– Were your senses reliable? I'm nowhere near that and I already feel my perception of colour changes from one day to the next.
– You are right to doubt. It remains the case that the celestials have nothing to do with life as it naturally exists on Earth, and that the further your perceptions extend, the more manifest their aberrations become.
– Such as, at random, being partly made of pure fire?
– Michael has a very particular thing about fire. It is rather his solution to every problem.
– And yet you seem to be on the same trip.
– You have the scientific background to conceptualise a disintegration, but in that era fire was the summit of the technological scale for me. I could imagine no greater destructive power, so I overused it whenever the situation grew tense.
– Had Ouro nothing better to offer?
– Ouro follows the evolution of human technology. At best. He does not precede it. Fire was likewise the summit of his science at the time and, in its variant based on striking stones together, it fascinated him at least as much as it did me.
– Right, but you must already have known about lightning too?
– A simple form of fire come down from the skies, from our point of view then. Electricity is a very modern idea.
– Shame, it would at least have added some variety. This fight is as boring as two big monsters, very strong, very tough and not very bright, slapping each other until one of them collapses with exhaustion.
– It was the beginning. We were all steeped in our own might, incapable of understanding that others might have an equivalent, and our idea of strategy did indeed rest on hitting ever harder.
– And at that game of who's the bigger pachyderm, you didn't come out on top.
– Indeed not. But you had guessed as much, or you would not be here.
– I was hoping there'd be clues in that fight that would let me do better if I ran into Micky myself, but apparently I'm asking too much.
– Yes. Michael is a force of nature in the literal sense. More than a plan, you need the power to move mountains.
– And where do I find that power, if even you with all those feathers got nowhere?
– I had an enormous amount of raw energy, but I used it carelessly. Later generations achieved far more destructive results with considerably fewer feathers.
– Hmm, that doesn't help me much. All I'm taking away is Ouro's utterly crestfallen face when you were finally burnt to a cinder. And his unkind comments beforehand.
– Ouro took time to learn self-control. For generations his true nature rose to the surface at the slightest setback. These days he is more polished.
– Ah. We were starting from low down.
– Yes. Do you want me to show him at his worst? Or shall we stop there?

– Are you not using your sword?
– I haven't got it.
– It is a purely imaginary confrontation. If you wish to summon it, you need only will it.
– Wouldn't that be cheating a bit? I didn't have it yet when the raiju killed me. Same for the disintegration.
– You did not have your regeneration either, nor physical capacities far beyond the limits of the human body, and yet you are using all of that to the full.
– I can't rein myself in to get back to my pre-pact level. It would be like unlearning how to walk or swim. Besides, in truth my memories of what I could and couldn't do before come down to some struggles with jam jars and a hundred-metre time from when I was sixteen.
– You got up again immediately after being struck by lightning. Three times. You are not going to tell me you think that might have been something you could do before?
– Never tested it. But this is different. I count it as a failure when I get fried, and I start the fight again from scratch.
– Ah, that explains the sensation of watching a great many takes of the same scene, strung together without transitions. You start again from the opening position as soon as you judge you ought to be dead.
– Yep.
– It is in no way representative of what the fight would have been had you stood your ground instead of backing towards the void, but it is an interesting handicapped training exercise. There may, however, be better moments to train than when a celestial mechanism is trying to kill you.
– You have to seize opportunities when they come. And it won't last long, I've finally got the trick.
– Which is?
– Go for the eyes.
– Indeed, the poor beast looks in a bad way. Even more so after you threw it over the parapet and it smashed down in exactly the spot where you ended up in real life.
– Gravity is universally merciless.
– May we now resume our investigations into what brought it here?
– I don't know. I'm hesitating about changing memory; all this rain and greyness is starting to wear me out.

Choice.text: Resume the investigation into the raiju

Page.Text:
– So, where can I go from here?
– More or less anywhere. The two obvious starting points are the ones you thought of first. Your meeting with Ouro. Your meeting with the eye.
– We're repeating ourselves, aren't we?
– Of course we are repeating ourselves. You are here to go over things until you understand.
– Have you nothing better to offer me?
– It is rather for you to offer. It is your mind, your memories. Have you no particular moment of your past in mind that seems worth digging into?
– My childhood? My wild youth?
– I was thinking rather of traumas.
– I've nearly died a fair few times, does that count? By fire, by ridicule…
– Do you not fail to die more or less constantly?
– I'm talking about events before the pact.
– Ah. Then yes, that could be interesting.
– Well, then.
– If your reflections have led you to discover one key of understanding or another, we can head in that direction too.
– Can we avoid the metaphors about keys and doors? They're overdone.
– The same applies if you have a precise idea in mind. And I am of course at your disposal for any questions you might have.
– I detect a passive-aggressive note in that last remark.
– I cannot stop you wasting your time, but I am still entitled to express my opinion about it.

The time I nearly died by ridicule
Follow the key of understanding I found
Follow the key of understanding I found
Follow the key of understanding I found
