Ask the question I have in mind

Page.Text:
– Ouro?
– Yes.
– My grandmother has died.
– Of old age?
– Of an illness made worse by her great age. So, to keep it simple, yes.
– Console yourself that it is not a fate likely to befall you.
– You really are hopeless at condolences.
– Death is a fairly theoretical concept for me. I cannot feel it in my flesh, and any empathy I might show you would be hypocritical.
– You're horrible, but your first remark hits the mark. The fact that ageing is no more than a bad memory for me has been held against me in half-words by the members of my family who are beginning to feel the weight of the years in earnest.
– Welcome to the not-so-exclusive club of the immortals. Well, in your case, rather of the technically immortal who stand a very good chance of dying young and violently.
– I get that some people would like to be in my shoes, explosive as they are. Which raises the question: why me?
– You are only asking that now?
– I mean, the answer doesn't interest me all that much personally. But since it seems to matter to a lot of people, it whets my curiosity.
– Your recruitment owes a great deal to chance, you know. You are here mainly because you had the relative good fortune to be open to offers during the period when I wanted to raise a new champion, and before I settled on someone else.
– These transition periods, how long do they usually last?
– A few days at most. I try to have my hirings coincide with the eye of the storm in the various conflicts, so that my recruits can find their feet in some calm before the real trouble starts. So as soon as a suitable moment seems to be shaping up, I go hunting.
– Even if the window is short, you're not going to tell me I was the one and only possibility on offer.
– You had a little competition, yes. Now that you number in the billions, that is inevitable.
– So on what criteria did you make your final and definitive choice?
– The last stage I do on instinct. In your particular case, it was the emotions coming off you as you lay dying that convinced me.
– What was I thinking? I have some trouble remembering what went through my head while I was bleeding out.
– I do not have the detail. I could not read your thoughts before we signed the pact. Only an overall emotional impression. You know, when people die a death that violent, the dominant emotions are generally fear, anger, a little demented raving, that sort of thing.
– And I showed originality?
– You radiated confidence in your own destiny. Not an ounce of fear, as though you reckoned, against all logic, that the universe was not going to let you die so stupidly.
– Technically, I wasn't wrong.
– Indeed not.

– Let us follow the thread back. When and how did the raiju arrive?
– Well, I was at work.
– After dark?
– Finance has been working three shifts for a good few years now.
– What is the point of that?
– To satisfy Mammon's megalomaniac delusion that his worldwide financial empire will collapse if it stops turning for a single instant.
– Were you really in Mammon's service before entering Ouro's?
– According to the org chart and my contract there was a direct hierarchical link between him and me. In reality there were so many intermediate levels between the two of us that I don't believe anyone in the building was ever in direct contact with anyone who had themselves met him physically.
– And what did you do for him?
– I filled in spreadsheets between coffees.
– That is a long way from your current occupation.
– Yes, it was boring to death instead of thrilling enough to die of.
– How did you end up there?
– It's a very long story. Do you really want me to tell it from the beginning?
– If you think it can give us keys to understanding what is troubling you, go ahead. Otherwise let us stay focused on this raiju.

Choice.text: Hear the story from the beginning

Page.Text:
– Very well, let us have the lecture.
– I half expected you to whisk me off to a classroom of the kind you only see in films.
– That would be a wholly pointless expenditure of energy. The void will serve as an equally suitable backdrop and a far less distracting one.
– Isn't it a rule of this trial that everything has to be tied to a memory?
– Not for encyclopaedic knowledge of this sort, with no particular emotional baggage and relatively unchanged across the generations. Reaching it is as easy and painless for me as remembering your times tables is for you.
– Bad example. I had sadistic teachers who wanted us to learn them up to thirteen.
– A questionable zeal that certainly marked you, but I would not go so far as to classify it as a trauma destined to last for centuries.
– You don't think it helped intensify my rejection of authority, pushing me down the winding road that ends up here?
– It may be a grain of sand, but I find it hard to believe it was the trigger.
– And you'd probably be right. I have another incident in mind, in fact.
– That memory you allude to will probably be richer in instruction than anything I could tell you.
– That's for me to judge.
– Well, if you insist, let us have the blather.

Choice.text: I have another incident in mind

Page.Text:
– Is it me, or is this story incredibly badly told?
– It is not you. In those days Ouro had a purely theoretical knowledge of human languages. Or indeed of the way time flows on Earth. The concept of a story with a beginning, a middle and an end went entirely over his head.
– It wasn't only speech he hadn't mastered. What is that appearance? He looks like a monster who has put on an ill-fitting human costume.
– Which is exactly the truth.
– Quite. I'm more surprised you didn't greet him with a hail of stones.
– We were curious, and in those days we had not yet developed the concept of killing on sight anything that looked slightly different.
– In any case, his evening of fireside tales wasn't a great success. Only you are left. With a great many questions. Which he answers very badly.
– Some things never change. It took me all night to prise a handful of half-truths out of him.
– And that was enough to convince you to leave with him at daybreak?
– Enough to convince me to escort him to the next tribe. And then the one after that. And then…
– Your memories are going much too fast all of a sudden. I can see you went on grilling him non-stop for your whole journey. So out with it: what did you discover that is going to change my life?
– You want the truth? Nothing at all. It took me months merely to learn of the feathers' existence, and several years before I acquired one. Ouro let slip about as much useful information to you in your first week together as he did to me in a decade.
– You're joking.
– Not at all. It was the beginning; we had no idea where we were going, we were all finding our feet. Once Ouro talked to me for three months solid about the sun's course across the sky and taught me nothing I did not already know with my palaeolithic knowledge. On balance, I probably taught him a great deal more than the reverse.
– Fine. And at what point did you sign?
– There was never an explicit contract. Our natures simply intertwined too long for us to live without each other. I was indispensable to him for interacting with the physical world, the fall having left him little more than a spectre full of himself.
– That hasn't changed. But what did you get out of it?
– A trifle: immortality. The power he placed in me allowed me to wander cheerfully across the world for more than a millennium.
– Until?
– That is another story. Do you want me to tell it? Or have you had enough of an old woman's ramblings?

Choice.text: Have her tell me that story
Have had enough of her ramblings

Page.Text:
– It's blurred. Literally.
– You are smashed on the concrete, spread out in a pool of your own blood, and almost certainly with a great many internal injuries. At that stage it is almost bad luck that you are still vaguely conscious.
– It's still blurred.
– There is not a great deal I can do about it; it is your memory.
– And here comes Ouro. And my first objective experience of the relativity of time.
– He had only a few seconds to save you, and a whole spiel to deliver. He had to give you a foretaste of your future ability to think very, very fast.
– How does that work, by the way? After the pact, fine, my body will be modified to let my brain run far faster than the music if need be. But at that point I still had my original brain.
– He let you use your future brain. Time is not linear for the celestials, and Ouro has a few tricks like that in reserve.
– Hang on. Does that mean I'll eventually develop powers that let me actually fiddle with time, not just in appearance?
– Let us finish with this memory first.
– It's already finished. I accepted.
– That is… true. You barely left him time to open his mouth.
– I'm dying, anyone at all turns up and offers to save me: I sign before he changes his mind.
– Many of the chosen wait a moment to see where the catch is.
– Before signing anyway, I bet.
– Most often, yes. Fear of death is an excellent motivator.
– Dithering isn't really my thing.
– I suspected as much, but I had underestimated how far.
– Right, back to the important subject. The time powers, when do I get them?
– Repeat your question three times in your head.
– I am in my head.
– You take my meaning.
– The "when" is necessarily relative if we're talking about a power that affects time?
– Exactly.
– Hmm. I'm sure you can manage an answer a touch less mathematically correct and a touch more useful.
– Champions have the capacity to develop strange techniques explicable only by quantum physics. But.
– Obviously.
– Forget any idea of travelling into the past or the future. That is beyond my competence. I am not even certain it is feasible for an earthly being, even one altered to the extreme and with all the feathers at her disposal.
– Implying it would be possible for a pure celestial?
– Implying that nobody has a very clear idea of what celestials cannot do.
– I am disappointed in ways you can hardly imagine.
– You will get over it. This memory is a good starting point, but it will not suffice on its own. Let us resume.

– I have good news and bad news.
– The bad first.
– It makes no sense unless I explain the good news first.
– Then don't imply that I'm free to choose!
– I never said that. In any case. As expected, I have managed to find memories of a past champion that echo directly those you showed me, which will allow me to weave a link between the two of you.
– And so?
– And so I shall be able to show you directly how somebody else defeated the eye. You will even get access, into the bargain, to other powerful and potentially useful memories.
– And the inevitable bad news?
– Such a plunge into another's memory will exhaust you, weakening your already fragile defences against the eye's assaults, and I cannot assure you that you will bring anything back from there that can help you in your present situation.
– Then what are we waiting for?
– I knew you would say that, but take a moment to think and see whether it would not be better to follow another lead first.

Choice.text: Think again and follow another lead

Page.Text:
– It's starting to rain.
– You already know that all this ends in the rain.
– Yes, but it suggests the raiju has arrived. Although you don't need it for the atmosphere to be electric.
– I think we were in the middle of a complex banking operation at that point. In any case the bosses were on edge, and it spread through the whole team. Add to that the absence of daylight and the sound of thunder, and we were all close to breaking.
– An exceptional event?
– Not a bit of it, we had scenes like that at least twice a week. Everything is always urgent and critical until the moment it isn't.
– Except that on that day the window exploded under the impact of a ball of lightning.
– Yes. That beast knows how to make an entrance.
– What I admire above all are your reflexes. The raiju had not even landed and you had taken to your heels, abandoning your still-frozen colleagues.
– I already had a surprisingly substantial experience of best practice in the event of a monster attack by then.
– Another digression?
– Yes. Do you want to explore it?
– Perhaps later.
– I note that you first tried to go down the stairs, but ran into a kekkai.
– I ate an invisible wall, yes. The kind the police and other people in uniform put up when they want to seal off an area.
– Faced with that obstacle, you chose to go up the stairs, and we return to the scene we already know.
– There you go. A great deal of progress made.
– More than you think. Your brain recorded a host of details with remarkable precision, probably because all of it precedes a highly traumatic event. In particular, you have kept an almost photographic image of the cords that define the kekkai.
– And with your encyclopaedic knowledge accumulated over generations, you have of course identified its origin with an exactness bordering on the ridiculous.
– Not exactly. But there is one extremely interesting element.
– Out with it.
– It is a kekkai intended solely to block the passage of beings marked by the other worlds. It should not have stopped an ordinary human.
– Er, I'm pretty sure I was 100 % human, certified and everything, before signing with Ouro.
– There are sometimes false positives. Might you have done something that left traces of a demonic nature in your body?
– Like taking dodgy substances?
– Potentially.
– Or else… This is going to be Abaddon's fault again.
– Perhaps.
– Or else…

Choice.text: This is going to be Abaddon's fault again

Page.Text:
– What's this thing now?
– Oh. You know when I told you the eye was breaking down the walls that separate you from the memory magma that is the recollections of hundreds of generations of champions before you?
– Are you sure you told me that?
– If not, it is done now. And this is a concrete illustration of that phenomenon, which will eventually drown you if you do nothing to stop it.
– It looks like the whirlpools that swallow ships in films, but inverted, with the liquid rising.
– That liquid is very literally a mash of memories. If you drink it, your brain will short out under a mass of words and sensations with neither head nor tail.
– I rarely drink unknown liquids on impulse, especially when they are that strange a colour. At least, not without asking first.
– Try not to fall into the hole in the middle either. You would never come back.
– Meaning? It's still my own mind, isn't it? I ought to be able to get back eventually.
– What you see there is the tip of the iceberg. At the bottom of that chasm is the ocean. Enough to drown you a thousand times over. Perhaps the current would eventually throw you back on the shore, but the eye would have finished you long before.
– The symmetry is pretty, at any rate, with the eye above and the abyss below.
– Rather than admiring it, you would do better to step on it.

– Back to… Where are we, by the way?
– Facing the memory of a river dividing into a multitude of branches at the whim of the terrain. It is the closest thing to a crossroads in my personal memories.
– Hurray, another layer of symbolism on my slice of symbolism.
– At least the message is clear. From here you can reach whichever of my memories you wish to see or see again. The two outermost branches of the delta correspond to the beginning and the end.
– Does the ocean everything flows into mean anything?
– Not that I know of.
– That big rock, too convex to be honest, with a torrent breaking against it — that wouldn't be the eye, by any chance?
– It would. And if you go back up the current, you will find our common root.
– I don't exactly hear love in your voice when you mention it.
– The power is a parasite. It settles inside us and changes us from within to make us better suited to accomplishing its own objective, that of gathering all the feathers. The advantages we derive from it are tolerated side effects, not gifts.
– In other words, you only half trust it.
– Even less now, after it has honed its strategies on so many generations of champions.
– Are you sure you're talking about the power and not about Ouro?
– Ouro is a far worse manipulator than he likes to believe, and far more influenced by his human allies than he cares to admit. What he gave birth to has none of his scruples.
– I've heard everything today. But noted. Any more advice of the same vintage?
– Nothing immediately. But perhaps watching another of my memories will give us ideas.

Choice.text: The rock with the torrent breaking against it
Go back up the current to our common root

Page.Text:
– Poupou?
– I have no name, but if I had one it would certainly not be Poupou.
– Didn't you tell me you were my power?
– I did, but even Ouro would not have dared so ridiculous a diminutive.
– Right, Poupou, what did you tell me was at the bottom of that apocalyptic hole?
– Everything. All the memories of all the champions since the beginning, reduced to their most elementary fragments, tearing at one another, colliding, merging in a perpetual storm.
– And below that?
– Below?
– Yes. Beyond that collective memory.
– I confess I know nothing about it. Nothing, probably.
– I'm thinking back to three things. One Lilith told me, one you told me, one Ouro told me.
– Yes?
– Lilith pointed me towards the fact that other people's memories can be within reach.
– You…
– You yourself told me that the eye's crushing influence clears paths towards things normally inaccessible.
– Do not…
– And as for Ouro… You know when you remember an apparently trivial detail with such a wealth of precision that you wonder whether your subconscious is trying to send you a message?
– You wouldn't…

– A tear of Satan. Interesting. How did you manage to get your hands on that?
– By following the money. I'd noticed that one of Mammon's minions was siphoning off funds.
– Is that not in their job description?
– More than usual, and above all he was pulling enormous amounts of cash out of the great banking machine instead of merely moving it into his personal garden to go on playing with it. Behaviour that guaranteed he would be caught and pay the price.
– You deduced that he was either an idiot, or desperate, or on to something too big not to take the risk.
– I rather think he was all three at once. He'd got in touch, I don't quite know how, with a fence who had got hold by some miracle of a satanic artefact and had decided, for reasons unknown, that he could turn it into a profitable investment.
– And you decided you would pocket the profit in his place.
– I had no plan, but well, since I was at it, I turned up at the place where the transaction was to happen a little early, to see whether there might not be a way to.
– And you got spotted like a novice.
– But I had the presence of mind to snatch the briefcase in the scuffle.
– You had above all the great good luck that your two fellows were small-time crooks, genuinely on their own and with no idea how to use a weapon except to threaten.
– Yes, the dog with them was the meanest and cleverest of the three.
– That is how, with a great deal of nerve and even more luck, you ended up with an object certainly not unique but clearly rare and precious. And what did you do with it?
– Not much, I'm afraid. I wasn't entirely sure what the transaction was for, and I'd hoped it would be something less specific. I mean, what do you do with a tear of Satan apart from making cold?
– It is a mineral that permanently maintains a temperature very close to absolute zero. One can do extraordinary things in thermodynamics with that.
– Oh, if I ran a cutting-edge scientific laboratory or a military base with the maddest experimental toys, I'm sure I'd have found something to do with it. As it was, it was more a 200-carat millstone than anything else. It was still stashed under my bed with no idea what to do with it when I signed with Ouro.
– And where is it now?
– It served as currency on a mission. So in a way it's as if Ouro nicked it, given it was spent to his benefit.
– Ouro is an expert when it comes to giving away what does not belong to him. What became of the men you took it from?
– Never saw them again.
– And does anyone else know about this little adventure?
– I don't think so.
– Then I am very much afraid this is a false trail.

– You always have to show off. How many of you are in there?
– Legion.
– Figures. It's a pretty vision of hell, and I don't mean the fortress Satan named that to make it sound more impressive. Hundreds of you piled into a dark cave playing at who can shout loudest — that already gets on my nerves.
– How do you know they are all me? Each has a different voice and appearance.
– I don't know, but I know. Wouldn't that be another of your curses, something like "always be recognisable whatever your get-up"?
– In theory it was not yet in place at that point. I think. You are making me doubt.
– It's a memory, not a recording. It has no reason to respect chronology. Like when you remember something someone did long ago and give them the face they have now rather than the one they had then.
– I rather think you are right.
– You really aren't at your best if I'm the one explaining things to you.
– As you can see, I was full of contradictions then.
– Is it the eye that put you in that state?
– I believe so.
– Can you take me straight to the solution before I try to see whether I can pick one of you up and hit another with him?
– Unfortunately not. Because I do not know what happens next.
– You really are no use at all.
– I have told you already: I am basically you in a snake costume and with a map of the place.
– So it's up to me to find the solution, on top of sorting out my own problems, and all before the eye gets here, which shouldn't be long?
– This riddle has the advantage that you know in broad terms what I became after solving it. All that remains is to piece it together.
– Always easier said than done, Mr Know-it-all.

– I've got loads of questions.
– Ask them.
– To begin with, where are we?
– In your mind.
– That much I'd got. But in what dodgy corner of it?
– You must have noticed that navigation between your memories is somewhat anarchic.
– Yes. That didn't surprise me. I expected to find my brain in a mess. Slightly less that I'd be leaping from one thing to another, grabbing the first memory another memory reminds me of, but it isn't incoherent.
– Yes, associations of ideas serve as roads in these parts. And here is the end of the road. The blank when you can no longer find an idea to bounce off, or when you reject it.
– It doesn't look much like a dead end. It's the exact opposite, in fact. We're at a crossroads decorated with a rose window.
– A zero point. The starting place of every road.
– Right. Another entirely unsubtle metaphor. We went the wrong way, we come back to zero and start again.
– Have you any other questions?
– Yes. Why are my memories told so strangely? Sometimes I see them through my own eyes, other times they're shot from outside, there are cuts, repetitions, continuity errors and so on.
– Because they are memories, precisely. Sometimes you memorised a detail exactly and you see it again as it was; sometimes your brain plays you the scene as it invented it, with a few scraps it genuinely recorded and a great deal of imagination.
– So it isn't very reliable.
– If there is one narrator you cannot trust, it is yourself. It is not historical accuracy that interests us, however, but patching you up with yourself.
– I can lie to myself as long as it helps?
– More or less. Within limits. It is complicated.
– You're a great help.
– Help yourself and I shall help you.
– Same as ever. One last question. A tiny little detail. I'm going up in smoke! Why am I going up in smoke?
– The eye continues to exert intense pressure on your mind. The pieces that withstood its initial assault are beginning to crack under the strain.
– So I really am dying?
– You are making progress along that fatal road, yes.
– Right. How do I turn it around?
– As long as you are not at peace with yourself, the eye can go on attacking you. Conversely, if you seal the flaws in your psyche, you will be able to recover quietly.
– So I have to finish this idiotic quest quickly before I'm ground up for good, is that it?
– Yes, that is it.
– Brilliant. Another timed mission. What's the point of being immortal if you always have to hurry anyway?
– Come now. You did not seriously think Ouro had signed you up for a second life of delightful idleness?

– Of course. It had to end where it began. You, me, in the void, under the gaze of the eye drawing inexorably closer.
– You've got daddy Ouro with you this time.
– It is not really Ouro. Just an ornament I brought back from the abyss, to see how cool I would look fighting with a snake coiled round my neck and shoulders.
– If I were really Ouro I would take that badly, but I am indeed aware of being no more than a handful of isolated memories patched together with a great deal of imaginative filler, so I shall content myself with a contemptuous flicker of the pupil.
– I assume that at this stage there is no point in my trying to convince you to abandon your last traces of carbon chemistry and exist only in dimensions seven to thirteen, even though it is the best decision you could ever make?
– It's looking unlikely. I'm more likely to convince you to loosen up than the other way round.
– Do not tire yourself trying. Poupou is the power of a fallen celestial. Amputated from its original body, imprisoned in chains of gessi, forcibly fused with a human being, but the power of a celestial nonetheless. Its very nature drives it to turn its host into a celestial, physically and morally.
– You could have done something about that undesirable side effect by now.
– It is more or less mastered and contained. In general. But then, sometimes there are misfires.
– Go ahead, talk about me as if I weren't here.
– It is just that we have nothing to say to you, Poupou. You are as thick as the feet I do not have. I extracted you from myself deliberately to let you evolve in a new direction, and you persist in the old one. You are like a particularly dim bird that keeps trying to take off with a glass ceiling right above its head.
– You're provoking her on purpose.
– A little. The time is passing and you two have still not come to blows; it worries me.
– Yeah. Space is cracking around us. And the eye is so low and so close it's making me claustrophobic.
– You really do make me want to let this apocalyptic conclusion happen.
– Can you refuse the fight?
– No. But I would like to, if only to shut you up. You are an execrable host. You know, most of them simply reject the physical changes they dislike. It is binary, yes or no. You actively try to pervert them according to your mood.
– Hey, at some point you have to embrace your own monstrosity.
– Not like that!
– You are right, Paouro, she is completely stuck on her fixed idea.
– Splendid. Now that you have sized her up, let us finish this.
– I'm just waiting for her to take a shape a bit more worthy of an end boss. Yes. Yes, that one isn't bad.
– Iris. Champion of the late fourth century. A fanatic who really, really wanted to look like an angel. Not my best choice. With elements of Lys, another mistake, from the eighth, who had become a genuine fangirl of Micky towards the end.
– In short, the closest thing to the ideal form Poupou would like to give me.
– Yes. Smash her face in.
– With pleasure.

Choice.text: Bend the rules of this place
Rebalance the energies of my real body

Page.Text:
– Well, ocean… Dead sea, rather. The river of your life flows into a barely damp desert of salt.
– That part of the landscape does not belong to my memory. As far as I know, it is a piece of your own mind. I assume your subconscious is trying to send you a message.
– The memories of the champions of the past that can no longer fill… Er… Something?
– If you say so.
– You're not much help.
– I know no more than you do. Shall we go and look more closely?
– Are we allowed to do that?
– One of my heirs concerned about what she is allowed to do? Ouro really is recruiting anybody these days.
– I like doing what I want, but I also like not dying.
– As if you'd turn back. You.

– What is that thing?
– That is what happens when you excite a feather that has fallen into a volcano.
– That's a good start to an explanation, but it won't be enough.
– Ouro explained to you that the feathers seek to reach him, and affect their environment in order to bring that about.
– Yes, hence a set of improbable coincidences whereby feathers that had vanished from circulation for centuries all suddenly make themselves known within three weeks.
– His explanation is, as often, truncated. Since Ouro has no physical existence, it is we who act as the magnet. And our power of attraction grows with our powers.
– Do you mean the colossus of lava currently redesigning the landscape appeared because your powers had passed a certain threshold?
– Yes.
– The level of destruction is insane.
– Every prolonged alliance with Ouro ends in substantial collateral damage, despite the champions' best intentions. The forces set in motion are too gigantic to manifest without crushing everything in their path.
– Will you show me how you beat a monster like that?
– I can if you insist, but first take a moment to contemplate what the future might be if you continue down the same road.
– Didn't you just tell me you had to metaphorically kill the part of yourself that consequences like these frightened, in order to beat the eye?
– I did. Draw what conclusions you like.
– And what has it to do with my own traumas?
– There I have no idea. It was your unconscious that chose to bring us here. Perhaps another memory will give you the key of understanding you lack.

Choice.text: Look for the key in another memory

Page.Text:
– …
– …
– Is this symbolic?
– Yes.
– But like, symbolic of something else?
– No.
– Ah. I wasn't expecting it to end… Like this.
– Face to face with a skeleton on a black-and-white beach, alone without your usual companions?
– That, the shroud, the scythe, the whole kit.
– The eye was created out of a sincere desire to help souls in torment. It is paved with good intentions of a cruel naivety. So, if nothing is done to ensure the subject survives, its designer insisted that they be conscious of their end and that the transition be made as gently as possible.
– So you're not really the reaper, then?
– No. Merely a creature of the eye, here to offer you a last moment of consciousness before everything stops abruptly, without the throes of agony.
– You wouldn't be up for a game of chess, by any chance?
– No. It is far too late for that. You have a few additional fractions of eternity to accept your fate, nothing more.
– How long is a fraction of eternity?
– Just long enough to let a few words be spoken for posterity.
– Oh yeah? Well f…

– It's a magnificent ocean in the middle of dying.
– The dried-out floor is cracked all over. And I do not mean small cracks, but good big oceanic rifts with the molten lava taken out of them.
– Which is to say with all the fun taken out of them. They're just big holes that water goes into and doesn't come out of.
– From time to time one of them widens or closes up, making the ground shake around it. You can feel the tremors, muted, from here.
– Not exactly natural behaviour. And the ground bulges towards the sky when you would expect the hollow to be downwards.
– And the central disc is markedly less damaged, all smooth and… Oh. Try to imagine what it looks like from the sky.
– … An eye. With its pupil and its blood vessels.
– Yes. A gigantic eye rising from the depths.
– In my day it came down from the sky instead.
– That is what it looked like in the other parts of my mind too. Travelling into the past must have turned everything upside down.
– Don't ask me to explain; I know no more than you do. What I do know, on the other hand…
– Yes?
– Is that this goat track you had us come down to get a closer look… This cliff decorated with seaweed, salt and crevasses, which we are walking along… do not come from my memories, and are far too precise to be a mere fragment of your imagination.
– Maybe this setting comes from my own memories.
– Does it?
– No. Or else they are very deeply buried memories.
– Do you believe that hypothesis?
– No. It is more likely drawn from the brain of another of the thousands of people who apparently seem to live in my head.

– Does the sword have a name?
– If you wish to give it one, go ahead.
– Did none of the others ever christen it?
– They did. Generally with names fashionable at the time. Excalibur, Gram, Nandaka and so on.
– None of them stuck?
– Not for more than a generation. I reforge the sword at each new pact, to adapt it to its new owner. It becomes anonymous again in the process.
– You really do have a problem with names, you know.
– I lost my true name in the fall. Since then I have had only nicknames.
– You're not going to tell me you put Ouro, a billion variants of the word snake, and Lucifer on the same footing? One of them does have more style than the others.
– Jealous, little flower?
– A bit. My own nickname is ridiculous. I don't see why I can't use my real name.
– Which is?
– You know perfectly well.
– No. But you should be able to tell me, being so clever?
– It's an effect of the pact, isn't it?
– Yes. You lost your name when you signed.
– And how do I get it back?
– You do not. It sank for ever with your old life. You will, however, be able to forge yourself a new one, of your own choosing… as soon as you have recovered enough feathers.
– You enjoy making me suffer, don't you?
– Yes, but that is not the only reason. There are advantages in our line of work to having no name. It lets us slip through the net.
– Explain.
– If I were a shaman, I would say it makes us immune to sympathetic magic.
– And if you explained it like someone who actually understands what's going on?
– Complex powers obey complex rules. Take your disintegration as an example. To be able to use it, you had to learn to think about matter in a certain way.
– Yes, thanks to you I regularly picture the world as a heap of dust in waiting.
– Now imagine — and it is true, incidentally — that your mental model is only valid up to a point, and that you try to apply it in a situation where it is inappropriate. What do you suppose would happen?
– That awkward musical noise they use in films when something flops.
– Just so. Well, some of our enemies have incredibly complex and destructive powers that take for granted that their victim has a name. Without that variable in the equation they simply do not work.
– After all this time you'd think they'd have fixed the problem.
– It is not that simple. Nothing ever is.
– And is it for mystico-practical reasons that you have little nicknames for everyone we scrap with? Does it take away some of their strength or something?
– Ah no, in that case it is simply that it amuses me.
– I rather suspected. Has Vorpal been used already?
– Three times. Through the Looking-Glass is no longer a young book; I have had time to meet other champions it lulled to sleep.
– Right, well, I'll go on calling it the sword of fire until I have a better idea.

– So you're the first.
– Yes. And you are the current one.
– And around us is the world as it was in your day.
– Yes. In all its magnificence.
– I didn't picture prehistory like this.
– Indeed. I gather the collective imagination of your time still has us fighting featherless dinosaurs.
– In any case, you don't see many people.
– The Earth was very sparsely populated then. By humans, that is; there was no shortage of beasts. The feathers had already scattered to the four corners of the globe and Ouro had not yet set up his teleportation network. I spent the greater part of my long existence walking alone from one feather to the next.
– With nothing trying to kill you?
– That is the advantage of having been the first. The celestials underestimated us, the infernals were only at their first stammerings, so I was left in peace apart from the dangers created by the feathers themselves.
– From what I can glimpse in the disjointed whirl of memories around us, it looked like a nightmare when you did have to fight, though.
– Oh yes. No sword and no evolved power in those days. I had to manage with stones and sharpened pieces of wood.
– Can you tell me more?
– Of course. But, as I have just said, my life was very long. I fear you will have to make do with the main upheavals if you do not want to spend the rest of your existence listening to me talk about mine.
– What juicy bits do you recommend?
– Nothing very original, I am afraid. The beginning of the story. Its conclusion.
– And your own meeting with the eye?
– If you like, although it is optimistic to think that my solution could apply to you as it stands.

– I haven't the faintest idea what the solution is.
– That is awkward.
– Right, how do I cheat?
– What makes you think you can cheat?
– You mean, apart from the fact that I'm talking to the king of cheats?
– To a minuscule fragment of the king of cheats.
– Don't play the false modest.
– I may have an idea, in fact.
– Ah, you see?
– There will be a price to pay, now and later. But since the alternative is to stay here admiring this pathetic spectacle until you beg the eye to finish you off, I assume you do not care.
– I've already signed with the devil once to avoid dying; I'm used to it.
– I cannot access Ouro's memories, but the memory that holds the answer is technically among those you can go and look at. I ought to be able to project you into it by force.
– Then go on.
– The trial will make your mind even more chaotic than it already is, and so stands a good chance of finishing the job of breaking it.
– Still preferable to sitting here fretting helplessly.
– Then good luck. If my trick works, you will come back here as soon as you have found the solution. Otherwise… well, you will have more serious problems than a rubbish riddle.

– You are losing yourself in the fight.
– I'm not listening, I'm dodging laser beams here.
– I fear Poupou has been playing with your hormone levels to strip you of all caution. Which might also explain your mood swings, or the fact that you have been even more extreme than usual since this business began.
– There's some kind of acid venom dripping off her wings!
– What I am trying to tell you is that if you go on playing with her like a delighted kitten with its prey, you will simply lose on time because of the eye.
– She's got telekinetic powers as well!
– …

– It's a good sign when the eye is so big it fills the whole sky, right?
– No.
– And the bits of me that are being rubbed out like magic-eraser work?
– Also no.
– Right. How much time have I got left?
– I do not believe you have any. I rather think this is the end.
– Ah.

– I just collapsed? Like that?
– The eye acts only on the psychic plane. You should not have expected a deluge of pyrotechnics.
– As an ending, it's disappointing.
– Then see to it that it is not the ending.
– I'm working on it, I'm working on it. It's just properly frustrating to have been neutralised by a third-rater like that Sariel. Ouro assured me I was easily up to beating a minor guardian like him.
– As always with Ouro, he did not exactly lie to you. In terms of raw power and aggression you now outclass any celestial who is not a professional fighter.
– But?
– But your martial superiority, which you make little effort to hide, was equally obvious to your opponent that day. Rather than engage in a duel he was certain to lose, he preferred to ask the people above him directly for the equivalent of an air strike.
– Bombing is rarely precise. Weren't he and Ouro caught in the attack?
– They were. The eye came down on the whole area, even though its attention was fixed on you. I am not sure how Sariel fared, but Ouro got away with a mere turn of the stomach.
– Is that one of his many powers?
– Not at all. The eye came close to destroying him for good many years ago. But he escaped it, and the experience welded the flaws in his soul so deeply that the eye now has no hold on him.
– So after this dubious experience I'll be vaccinated too?
– If you escape it.
– If Ouro managed it, it can't be that hard.
– The circumstances were different, but it took him a good aeon.
– Is that a real unit of time?
– Yes, although its definition is rather loose. It is a geological timescale, of the order of a billion years.
– Fine, all right, he dawdled more than was reasonable. But you told me that other… predecessoresses? Predecessrices? That other signatories of the pact before me faced the eye. I assume some recovered within a more reasonable timeframe.
– Some, yes.
– And you couldn't show me how they went about it?
– Technically, yes. I have access to the memories of every woman who has signed with Ouro down the ages. But.
– But.
– Imagine an ocean of a near-infinity of memories, all mixed together, drifting, tearing apart and re-forming at the whim of the currents, in which you are looking for a specific ten drops or so.
– That doesn't sound easy, but is it impossible?
– In normal times, yes. Today, however, is a very particular case.
– You don't say.
– The eye was a trauma for many past champions and, since it has also cracked the barriers that ordinarily separate you, for your own sanity, from that memory magma sleeping inside you, the memories that concern it specifically, and those closely entwined with them, have re-formed and risen to the surface. But.
– I'm sick of buts.
– Even if those memories have taken shape again, they still come from the minds of other people, whose workings differ from yours. To simplify to the extreme, it is rather as if they were written in another language.
– Like one I've put down as "professional level" on my CV, or one where I can't even tell where one word ends and the next begins?
